analysis.one_liner: Bans nursing homes from forcing residents to sign away their right to sue before disputes arise.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 31 cosponsors but never got a vote, dying in a House Judiciary subcommittee after being referred in February 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it unenforceable for a nursing home or assisted living facility to require a resident to agree to private arbitration before any dispute arises. Such agreements, often signed during the stressful admission process, typically force families into a private arbitrator instead of court, where cases are public and juries can award damages. The bill would let residents and their families decide after a dispute occurs whether to arbitrate or sue.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future nursing home residents and their families. They could refuse or ignore arbitration clauses signed at admission and take claims of neglect, abuse, or wrongful death to court, where proceedings are public and juries can award full damages.

how_it_helps.text: Lets nursing home residents and their families keep their right to go to court instead of being locked into private arbitration by a contract signed before any dispute exists.
Covers agreements signed during or after admission, so facilities could not work around the ban by getting signatures later in the stay.
Makes a court, not an arbitrator, the judge of whether the ban applies, closing a common loophole where arbitrators decide their own authority.

analysis.who_pays: Nursing homes and other long-term care facilities, which could no longer require residents to sign away their right to a day in court before disputes arise, and would face more lawsuits and trials in cases of alleged neglect or abuse.

drawbacks.text: Arbitration can be faster and cheaper than court for families with smaller claims, and the bill bans even voluntarily chosen pre-dispute arbitration, not just coerced agreements.
The long-term care industry argues arbitration keeps dispute costs down, which facilities say helps keep care affordable; the bill would remove that option entirely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit runs to a vulnerable group: people entering nursing homes, often in crisis and with little bargaining power, would no longer be bound by contracts they signed before any dispute existed. The cost falls on the industry, which faces greater litigation exposure and loses a cheaper dispute channel. The strongest objection is that the ban also covers arbitration both sides might genuinely prefer for speed and cost. Weighing that, the bill is a modest, targeted consumer protection; its main failure is procedural, not substantive — it never even got a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee for over a year, never got a markup or a floor vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 26, 2009, by Rep. Linda T. Sánchez with 8 original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to the Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law, where it sat for over a year.
On June 21, 2010, the subcommittee was discharged from further consideration, but the bill never advanced to the full committee or the House floor and received no vote before the Congress ended.
Thirty-one members, including 2 Republicans, cosponsored the bill, but that support was never converted into floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing homes and long-term care operators are better off, because they can continue using arbitration clauses that keep disputes out of court. Residents and families remain no better off than before.

for.name: Rep. Linda T. Sánchez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led the effort to bar pre-dispute arbitration agreements in long-term care facilities.

for.name: 31 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill: 29 House Democrats and 2 House Republicans signed on.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: House Judiciary Committee, chaired by Rep. John Conyers
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never brought it to a vote or advanced it to the full committee.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic (29 of 31 cosponsors) but included 2 Republicans, and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and long-term care facilities
industries.note: The bill would stop these facilities from requiring residents to sign arbitration clauses at admission, which typically prevent families from suing over neglect, abuse, or wrongful death and keep such cases out of public court. Losing that shield means more lawsuits and jury exposure.
Arbitration firms and lawyers who administer nursing home disputes under pre-dispute clauses would lose a stream of cases routed to them instead of the courts.
